# Benign bone tumors

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Surgery > Trauma and orthopedic surgery > Neoplasia > Benign bone tumors*

[Original Article Link](/library/7Q04xf)

---

## Summary

Benign bone lesions are a heterogeneous group of slow-growing <u>neoplasms</u> that arise from <u>cartilage</u> or bone. They appear on <u>x-ray</u> as localized lesions with sharp margins and without <u>soft tissue</u> involvement. Surgical removal or <u>curettage</u> may be required to manage <u>pain</u> and/or prevent <u>pathological fractures</u>.

---

## Overview of benign bone tumors

Benign bone tumors are usually asymptomatic and do not require treatment until they become symptomatic (<u>pain</u>, swelling, etc). <u>Surgery</u> is indicated for symptomatic lesions and may involve <u>curettage</u>, bone grafting, or resection.




### Predominantly osseous tumors




| Overview of predominantly osseous tumors |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Type | Description | <u>Epidemiology</u> | Location | Characteristics |
| <u>Osteoid osteoma</u> | <br>* Small, predominantly cortical <u>tumor</u> (< 2 cm)<br><br> | <br><br>* Peak <u>incidence</u>: 4–25 years<br><br>* Sex: <u>♂</u> > <u>♀</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Metaphysis</u> and <u>diaphysis</u> of <u>long bones</u><br><br>* <u>Vertebrae</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Severe nocturnal bone <u>pain</u><br><br>* <u>Pain</u> responds to <u>NSAIDs</u><br><br>* <u>X-ray</u>: <u>radiolucent</u> core (<u>osteoid</u>), surrounded by perifocal <u>sclerosis</u><br><br>* <u>Surgery</u> is necessary if <u>pain</u> becomes unresponsive to medication.<br><br><br> |
| <u>Osteoblastoma</u> | <br>* Predominantly cortical <u>tumor</u> larger than <u>osteoid osteoma</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Peak <u>incidence</u>: 10–20 years<br><br>* Sex: <u>♂</u> > <u>♀</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Vertebrae</u> (predominantly <u>posterior column</u>)<br><br> | <br><br>* Severe <u>chronic pain</u> (not nocturnal) that is unresponsive to <u>NSAIDs</u><br><br>* <u>X-ray</u>: central lucent nidus with mild or absent perifocal <u>sclerosis</u><br><br><br> |
| Giant-cell <u>tumor</u> (<u>osteoclastoma</u>) | <br>* <u>Tumor</u> arising from <u>giant cells</u> of the <u>bone marrow</u><br><br> | <br>* Peak <u>incidence</u>: 20–40 years<br><br> | <br>* <u>Epiphysis</u> of <u>long bones</u> (usually around the knee)<br><br> | <br><br>* Local <u>pain</u> and swelling<br><br>* <u>Pathological fractures</u><br><br>* <u>X-ray</u>: multicystic <u>osteolytic lesions</u> (soap-bubble appearance)<br><br>* <u>Histopathology</u>: <u>multinucleated giant cells</u> and mononuclear, <u>RANKL</u>-expressing cells<br><br>* Locally aggressive <u>tumor</u><br><br>* Risk of malignant degeneration increases with age.<br><br><br> |
| <u>Osteoma</u> | <br>* Well-defined solitary <u>tumor</u>, usually with a diameter < 1 cm that arises from <u>osteoblasts</u><br><br> | <br>* Peak <u>incidence</u>: middle age<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Facial bones</u> and <u>cranial bones</u>, especially <u>paranasal sinuses</u><br><br>* <u>Long bones</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Usually asymptomatic<br><br>* A nasal sinus <u>osteoma</u> may result in obstruction of the ostium, with subsequent congestion and pressure <u>headaches</u>.<br><br>* Associated with <u>Gardner syndrome</u><br><br><br> |
| Torus palatinus | <br>* Benign bony overgrowth of the <u>hard palate</u><br><br> | <br>* Peak <u>incidence</u>: young adults<br><br> | <br>* Roof of the mouth (midline <u>hard palate</u>)<br><br> | <br><br>* Usually asymptomatic and requires no treatment<br><br>* If it interferes with speech or eating, <u>surgery</u> is an option.<br><br><br> |

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | Description | <u>Epidemiology</u> | Location | Characteristics |
| (<u>Distal</u>) <u>enchondroma</u> | <br>* <u>Tumor</u> arising from <u>hyaline cartilage</u><br><br> | <br>* Peak <u>incidence</u>: 20–50 years<br><br> | <br>* Medulla of the long <u>bones of the hand</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Usually asymptomatic<br><br>* Possibly, local widening or <u>pathological fractures</u><br><br>* Variants: <u>enchondromatosis</u><br><br>* Predominantly hereditary; multiple <u>enchondromas</u><br><br>* Peak <u>incidence</u>: 10–20 years<br><br>* Often leads to skeletal deformities and stunted growth<br><br>* Increased risk of malignant degeneration into <u>chondrosarcoma</u><br><br><br> |
| <u>Chondroblastoma</u> | <br>* Very rare <u>cartilage</u> <u>tumor</u><br><br> | <br>* Peak <u>incidence</u>: 10–20 years<br><br> | <br>* <u>Epiphysis</u> of the <u>long bones</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Joint</u> <u>pain</u> and swelling<br><br> |
| <u>Synovial chondromatosis</u> | <br>* Enchondral formation of <u>cartilage</u> as a result of <u>metaplasia</u> of synovial tissue<br><br> | <br>* Peak <u>incidence</u>: 20–40 years<br><br> | <br>* Most commonly <u>the knee joint</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Pain</u>, effusion, knee locking<br><br>* Radiographically visible loose bodies<br><br>* Malignant degeneration to synovial <u>chondrosarcoma</u> in extremely rare cases<br><br><br> |
| <u>Osteochondroma</u> (<u>cartilaginous exostosis</u>) | <br>* <u>Bony exostosis</u> with <u>cartilage</u> cap<br><br> | <br><br>* Peak <u>incidence</u>: 10–30 years<br><br>* Sex: <u>♂</u> > <u>♀</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Metaphysis</u> of <u>long bones</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Most common primary benign bone <u>tumor</u><br><br>* Usually asymptomatic, but can be painful and palpable near the ends of <u>long bones</u><br><br>* <u>X-ray</u>: pediculated or <u>sessile</u> mass<br><br>* Disease variant: <u>hereditary multiple exostoses</u> (malignant degeneration may occur)<br><br>* Transformation into <u>chondrosarcoma</u> is rare<br><br><br> |

| Overview of <u>fibromas</u> |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | Description | <u>Epidemiology</u> | Location | Characteristics |
| <u>Nonossifying fibroma</u> | <br>* Fibrous growth in areas that normally ossify<br><br> | <br>* Peak <u>incidence</u>: 10–20 years<br><br> | <br>* Metaphyseal; very common in the <u>distal</u> <u>femur</u> and <u>distal</u> <u>tibia</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Usually an incidental finding<br><br>* <u>X-ray</u><br><br>* Marginal <u>sclerosis</u><br><br>* Lobulated structures with translucent components<br><br><br> |
| <u>Ossifying fibroma</u> | <br>* <u>Fibrous bone</u> <u>tumor</u><br><br> | <br>* Peak <u>incidence</u>: 1–5 years<br><br> | <br>* <u>Tibia</u> and <u>fibula</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Localized swelling<br><br>* Tibial bowing<br><br>* <u>Pathological fractures</u> may occur.<br><br>* <u>X-ray</u>: intracortical, <u>osteolytic lesions</u> with interspersed <u>sclerosis</u><br><br><br> |
| <u>Fibrous dysplasia</u> | <br>* Normal skeletal tissue is replaced by fibrous tissue<br><br> | <br>* Peak <u>incidence</u>: <u>adolescence</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Monostotic</u> <u>fibrous dysplasia</u>: <u>long bones</u>, <u>facial bones</u> (∼ 70% of cases)<br><br> | <br><br>* Often asymptomatic; may cause bone <u>pain</u><br><br>* <u>X-ray</u><br><br>* <u>Long bones</u>: well-defined, lobulated lytic lesions with a thin cortex and a <u>radiolucent</u>, ground-glass appearance<br><br>* <u>Facial bones</u>: radiodense lesions with a leonine appearance<br><br><br> |





### Cysts and <u>hemangiomas</u>




| Overview cysts and hemangiomas |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Type | Description | <u>Epidemiology</u> | Location | Characteristics |
| <u>Unicameral bone cyst</u> | <br>* Solitary, generally single-chambered bone cysts<br><br> | <br>* Peak <u>incidence</u>: 5–15 years<br><br> | <br>* <u>Metaphysis</u> of the <u>long bones</u> (predominantly the <u>proximal</u> <u>humerus</u> and <u>proximal</u> <u>femur</u>)<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Pathological fractures</u><br><br>* <u>X-ray</u>: <u>osteolytic bone lesion</u> with sharp margins and no <u>sclerosis</u> in the <u>metaphysis</u> of <u>long bones</u><br><br>* <u>Aspiration</u> and <u>corticosteroid</u> injection for larger lesions<br><br>* Fallen fragment sign: characteristic radiological finding in which a bone <u>fracture</u> fragment appears within the cavity of a bone cyst<br><br><br> |
| <u>Aneurysmal bone cyst</u> | <br>* Mostly septated, blood-filled cysts<br><br> | <br>* Peak <u>incidence</u>: 10–20 years<br><br> | <br><br>* May affect any bone<br><br>* Most common localizations: <u>spine</u> and <u>metaphysis</u> of the <u>long bones</u><br><br>* Predominantly affects the lower extremities<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Local <u>pain</u> and swelling may occur.<br><br>* <u>X-ray</u>: <u>osteolytic lesion</u> with definite margins; usually located in the <u>metaphysis</u><br><br>* <u>MRI</u>: multichambered lesion with fluid-fluid levels<br><br>* High risk of recurrence<br><br><br> |
| <u>Intraosseous hemangioma</u> | <br>* Vascular <u>neoplasm</u><br><br> | <br>* Peak <u>incidence</u>: 30–50 years<br><br> | <br><br>* Most common <u>benign tumor</u> of the <u>spine</u><br><br>* Particularly involves the thoracic and <u>lumbar vertebrae</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Possible complications: compression <u>fractures</u>, <u>spinal stenosis</u>, bleeding resulting in <u>spinal epidural hematoma</u><br><br>* <u>X-ray</u><br><br>* Vertically streaked <u>vertebrae</u>;<br><br>* Honeycomb appearance of lesions with definite margins<br><br><br> |
| <br><u>Langerhans cell histiocytosis</u> <br> | <br>* Lytic lesion consisting of Langerhans and <u>immune cells</u><br><br> | <br>* Peak <u>incidence</u>: 5–10 years<br><br> | <br>* Most commonly in the <u>skull</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Painful swelling<br><br>* <u>Pathologic fracture</u><br><br>* <u>X-ray</u>: <u>osteolytic lesions</u> with or without marginal <u>sclerosis</u><br><br>* Typically, solitary lesions<br><br>* May manifest with <u>rash</u> and recurrent <u>otitis media</u> with mastoid swelling<br><br>* Lesions near the <u>sphenoid</u>, orbital, <u>ethmoid</u>, or <u>temporal bones</u> require treatment with <u>vinblastine</u> and <u>prednisone</u>.<br><br><br> |

## Giant-cell tumor of bone (osteoclastoma)

* Description: benign but locally aggressive <u>tumor</u> composed of <u>giant cells</u> that arise from the <u>bone marrow</u> [[1]](/library/8s0O9h)

* <u>Epidemiology</u>: peak <u>incidence</u> between 20 and 40 years

* Clinical features

* Found in the <u>epiphysis</u> or <u>metaphysis</u> of <u>long bones</u> (especially knee region)

* <u>Pathological fractures</u>

* Local <u>pain</u> and swelling

* Limited <u>range of motion</u>

* Diagnostics

* <u>X-ray</u>: multicystic <u>osteolytic</u> lesions (soap-bubble appearance)

* <u>Histopathology</u>

* Mononuclear, <u>RANKL</u>-expressing cells (<u>neoplastic</u>)

* <u>Multinucleated giant cells</u> (are reactive and resemble <u>osteoclasts</u>)

* Treatment: <u>curettage</u> and bone grafting or en-bloc resection to minimize recurrence rate

* Prognosis: risk of malignant degeneration increases with age; may spread to the <u>lungs</u>





![Bubbly bone lesion](media/vuyxfsue768c2q5w76kjmild.jpg)

Bubbly bone lesion

![Giant-cell tumor of the bone (osteoclastoma)](media/aujk4mqevo5p8do12elnl2pe.jpg)

Giant-cell tumor of the bone (osteoclastoma)

## Osteochondroma (cartilaginous exostosis)

* Description

* Bony outgrowth (exostosis) with a <u>cartilaginous</u> cap on the surface of <u>long bones</u> adjacent to <u>growth plates</u>

* Contains a marrow space that is continuous with the underlying bone

* <u>Epidemiology</u>

* Most common primary benign bone <u>tumor</u>

* Peak <u>incidence</u>: 10–30 years [[2]](/library/cfbaOG)

* Sex: <u>♂</u> > <u>♀</u>

* Clinical features

* Typically located in <u>metaphysis</u> of <u>long bones</u>

* Usually asymptomatic, but can be painful and palpable near the ends of <u>long bones</u>

* Subtypes and variants: hereditary multiple exostoses (EXT)

* Definition: <u>autosomal dominant</u> disorder with multiple exostoses

* Most commonly caused by <u>autosomal dominant inheritance</u> of a <u>germline mutation</u> in the EXT <u>tumor suppressor gene</u>.

* Malignant degeneration to <u>chondrosarcoma</u> may occur (∼ 5% of cases).

* Diagnostics: <u>x-ray</u> shows <u>pedunculated</u>;   or <u>sessile</u>;   lesion on the surface of the <u>metaphysis</u> of <u>long bones</u>

* Treatment: excision of <u>tumor</u> in symptomatic cases

* Complications: Approx. 1% transform into <u>chondrosarcoma</u>.

## Enchondroma

* Description: <u>benign tumor</u> arising from <u>hyaline cartilage</u>

* <u>Epidemiology</u>

* Most common type of hand <u>tumor</u>

* Peak <u>incidence</u>: 20–50 years (but may occur at any age)

* Clinical features

* Usually found in medulla of the <u>long bones</u> of the hands and feet (most often the <u>metacarpals</u> of the hand and <u>phalanges</u> of the fingers)

* Often painless

* Widening of the bone

* Pathological (spontaneous) <u>fractures</u>

* Subtypes and variants: enchondromatosis  [[3]](/library/LKXwS_)

* Definition: A predominantly hereditary condition that manifests with multiple <u>enchondromas</u>.

* <u>Epidemiology</u>: peak <u>incidence</u> between 10 and 20 years

* Clinical features: often leads to skeletal deformities and stunted growth

* Prognosis: increased risk of malignant degeneration to <u>chondrosarcoma</u>

* Treatment

* Asymptomatic tumors do not require treatment and close monitoring suffices.

* Symptomatic tumors may require surgical <u>curettage</u> and subsequent bone grafting to prevent <u>pathological fractures</u>.





![Enchondroma of the fifth metacarpal of the left hand](media/f1h1hxmpepyu3ndi3mp2mzuz.jpg)

Enchondroma of the fifth metacarpal of the left hand

![Enchondroma (enchondromatosis)](media/gcv4vrm139cztdmr6lfvwfvl.jpg)

## Synovial chondromatosis

* Description: <u>cartilage</u> formation as a result of <u>metaplasia</u> of the synovial tissue

* <u>Epidemiology</u>: peak <u>incidence</u> between 20 and 40 years

* Clinical features

* Most commonly located in the knees

* <u>Pain</u>, effusion, reduced <u>range of motion</u>, knee locking

* Diagnostics: <u>x-ray</u> shows radiographically visible (calcified) loose bodies

* Treatment: removal of loose bodies and synovial tissue

* Prognosis: extremely low risk of malignant degeneration to synovial <u>chondrosarcoma</u>





![Synovial chondromatosis](media/r8r5k77c02ascskwrz0e2v8d.jpg)

Synovial chondromatosis

## Osteoid osteoma and osteoblastoma

### Osteoid osteoma [[4]](/library/rSYfaK)




* Description

* Small <u>tumor</u> (< 2 cm)

* Predominantly located in the cortex of <u>long bones</u>

* <u>Epidemiology</u>

* Peak <u>incidence</u>: 4–25 years [[5]](/library/Xfb9kG)

* Sex: <u>♂</u> > <u>♀</u>

* Clinical features

* Located in <u>metaphysis</u> and <u>diaphysis</u> of <u>long bones</u> (predominantly the <u>proximal</u> <u>femur</u>, <u>tibia</u>, and <u>humerus</u>) and <u>vertebrae</u>

* Constant, intense <u>pain</u> that worsens at night

* <u>Pain</u> is responsive to <u>NSAIDs</u> (e.g., <u>ibuprofen</u>, <u>aspirin</u>)

* Diagnostics

* <u>X-ray</u> or CT: <u>radiolucent</u> core (<u>osteoid</u>), surrounded by perifocal <u>sclerosis</u> (nidus)

* <u>Scintigraphy</u>: usually intense <u>enhancement</u>

* Double-density sign

* Intraoperative nuclear imaging using a probe to detect the <u>tumor</u>

* Treatment: <u>NSAIDs</u> or surgical removal if <u>pain</u> is unresponsive to medical treatment





![Osteoid osteoma](media/ailgyld5cluz8hsisfgkh43y.jpg)

Osteoid osteoma

![Osteoid osteoma of the fibula](media/m8lpln58qya9d4kn8hrfdns4.jpg)

Osteoid osteoma of the fibula

![Osteoid osteoma of the acetabulum](media/klm8r0t8zz84l3m4qfv5aykv.jpg)

Osteoid osteoma of the acetabulum




### Osteoblastoma [[6]](/library/7SY4aK)




* Description: predominantly cortical <u>tumor</u> larger than <u>osteoid osteoma</u> (> 2 cm)

* <u>Epidemiology</u>

* Peak <u>incidence</u>: 10–20 years

* Sex: <u>♂</u> > <u>♀</u>

* Clinical features

* Typically involves the <u>posterior</u> elements of the <u>vertebrae</u> (<u>vertebral arch</u>)

* Severe chronic local <u>pain</u> (no nocturnal <u>pain</u>) that does not respond to <u>NSAIDs</u>

* Neurologic symptoms if the spinal cord is compressed

* Diagnostics: <u>x-ray</u>

* Shows <u>tumor</u> located in the <u>cortical bone</u>

* Central lucent nidus with mild or absent perifocal <u>sclerosis</u>

* Treatment

* Unresponsive to <u>NSAIDs</u>

* Surgical <u>curettage</u> and bone grafting preferred





![Osteoblastoma cervical spine](media/r9v521uc2dc32knrtuda3oyt.jpg)

Osteoblastoma cervical spine

## Osteoma

* Description: benign round bone <u>tumor</u>

* <u>Epidemiology</u>: most common in middle-aged individuals but may develop at any age

* Etiology: associated with <u>Gardner syndrome</u>

* Clinical features

* Usually affects facial bones and <u>cranial bones</u> (most commonly affects <u>paranasal sinuses</u>)

* In rare cases, <u>long bones</u>

* Often asymptomatic

* An <u>osteoma</u> of the paranasal sinus may lead to obstruction of the ostium, with subsequent congestion and pressure <u>headaches</u>.

* Associated with <u>Gardner syndrome</u>: extracolonic manifestation of <u>familial adenomatous polyposis</u> (<u>FAP</u>) that includes <u>osteomas</u> of the <u>skull</u> or <u>mandible</u>, <u>hypertrophy</u> of the <u>retinal pigment epithelium</u>, <u>adrenal adenomas</u>, <u>desmoid tumors</u>, dental abnormalities, and cutaneous lesions

* Treatment: Surgical removal may be required if expansive <u>tumor</u> growth leads to symptoms.





![Osteoma of the frontal sinus](media/w3lqgoq9kfpwo7a80srrrmuq.jpg)

Osteoma of the frontal sinus




> [!NOTE]
> <u>Osteomas</u> of the <u>skull</u> and <u>mandible</u> in conjunction with <u>hypertrophy</u> of the <u>retinal pigment epithelium</u>, <u>adrenal adenomas</u>, <u>desmoid tumors</u>, and dental abnormalities are characteristic of <u>Gardner syndrome</u>.

---

## Nonossifying fibroma

* Description: growth of fibrous <u>connective tissue</u> into areas that normally ossify; a <u>tumor</u>-like lesion that is considered to be a nonneoplastic disorder of bone growth, rather than a true <u>neoplasm</u>

* <u>Epidemiology</u>: peak <u>incidence</u> between 10 and 20 years

* Clinical features

* Usually metaphyseal (predominantly in the <u>distal</u> <u>femur</u> and <u>distal</u> <u>tibia</u>)

* asymptomatic; usually an incidental finding [[7]](/library/R5XlPA)[[8]](/library/i5XJPA)

* Diagnostics: <u>x-ray</u> 

* Marginal <u>sclerosis</u>

* Lobulated structure with translucent components

* Treatment

* Usually <u>self-limiting</u>

* Bone grafting may be required for painful lesions or to prevent <u>pathological fractures</u>.

## Fibrous dysplasia

* Description: <u>Fibrous dysplasia</u> is a benign, developmental disorder of bone that causes normal skeletal tissue to be replaced by fibrous tissue.

* <u>Epidemiology</u>

* <u>Fibrous dysplasia</u> accounts for approx. 5% of benign bone lesions

* Age of onset: most commonly presents during <u>adolescence</u>

* Sex: <u>♂</u> = <u>♀</u>

* Etiology: post-zygotically acquired, somatic, <u>gain-of-function</u> mutation in GNAS1 <u>gene</u> on <u>chromosome</u> 20q

* Pathophysiology

* GNAS1 codes for the α subunit of the <u>G<sub>s</sub> protein</u> (G<sub>s</sub>α).

* Mutation → constitutive activation of certain Gs-<u>cAMP</u> coupled pathways → inhibition of <u>mesenchymal</u> differentiation into <u>osteoblasts</u> → lack of <u>osteocytes</u>  → skeletal lesions composed largely of <u>mesenchymal</u> cells → weak, imperfect bone with fibrous tissue

* Clinical features

* Disease <u>phenotype</u> 

* <u>Monostotic</u> <u>fibrous dysplasia</u> (∼ 70% of cases)

* <u>Polyostotic</u> <u>fibrous dysplasia</u> (∼ 25% of cases)

* Common to all disease <u>phenotypes</u>

* Bone <u>pain</u>, bone deformities, and/or <u>pathological fractures</u>

* <u>Entrapment neuropathies</u> may occur as a result of expanding bone lesions

* Age at manifestation

* <u>Monostotic</u> <u>fibrous dysplasia</u>: 20–30 years

* <u>Polyostotic</u> <u>fibrous dysplasia</u>: < 10 years

* Diagnostics

* Laboratory tests

* ↑ <u>Alkaline phosphatase</u> (occasionally)

* Normal <u>calcium</u>, <u>PTH</u>, and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D levels

* Imaging: <u>x-ray</u>

* <u>Long bones</u>: well-defined, lobulated lesions with a thin cortex and a <u>radiolucent</u>, ground-glass appearance

* <u>Facial bones</u>: radiodense lesions with a leonine appearance

* Pathology: <u>bone biopsy</u>

* Therapy 

* <u>Bisphosphonates</u>

* Management of <u>precocious puberty</u>: See “<u>Peripheral precocious puberty</u>.”

* Prognosis

* The lesions do not heal spontaneously.

* <u>Osteosarcomas</u> occur in < 1% of cases.





References:[[9]](/library/Nl0-CT)




### Syndromes associated with <u>polyostotic</u> <u>fibrous dysplasia</u>




* <u>McCune-Albright syndrome</u>

* <u>Polyostotic</u> <u>fibrous dysplasia</u>

* <u>Café au lait spots</u> with unilateral, ragged edges

* Most commonly peripheral <u>precocious puberty</u>

* Mazabraud syndrome

* <u>Polyostotic</u> <u>fibrous dysplasia</u>

* Intramuscular <u>myxomas</u>

* Jaffe-Lichtenstein syndrome

* <u>Café au lait spots</u>

* <u>Polyostotic</u> <u>fibrous dysplasia</u>

## Aneurysmal bone cysts

* Description

* <u>Osteolytic lesions</u>; usually septated, blood-filled cysts

* <u>Idiopathic</u> (primary <u>aneurysmal bone cyst</u>) or secondary to malignant or other benign bone diseases (secondary <u>aneurysmal bone cyst</u>)

* <u>Epidemiology</u>: peak <u>incidence</u> between 10 and 20 years

* Clinical features

* Common sites are the <u>spine</u> and the <u>metaphysis</u> of the <u>femur</u> and <u>tibia</u>.

* Usually asymptomatic; local <u>pain</u> and swelling may occur

* <u>Pathological fracture</u>: often the first sign

* Diagnostics

* <u>X-ray</u>: metaphyseal, <u>osteolytic lesion</u> with <u>sclerotic</u> margins

* <u>MRI</u> : septated, blood-filled lesions, with typical fluid-fluid levels.

* Treatment: surgical <u>curettage</u> and bone grafting

* Prognosis: high risk of recurrence

## Intraosseous hemangioma

* Description: vascular <u>neoplasm</u> [[10]](/library/8SYOYK)

* <u>Epidemiology</u>

* Peak <u>incidence</u>: 30–50 years

* Sex: <u>♂</u> < <u>♀</u> (1:2)

* Clinical features

* Most common <u>benign tumor</u> of the <u>spine</u>, particularly in the thoracic and <u>lumbar vertebrae</u>

* Usually asymptomatic; often an incidental finding

* Diagnostics: <u>x-ray</u> 

* Vertical streaks visible in <u>vertebrae</u>

* Honeycomb appearance of lesion with sharp margins

* Treatment: usually no treatment required

* Complications

* Compression <u>fractures</u>

* <u>Spinal stenosis</u>

* Bleeding with subsequent <u>spinal epidural hematoma</u>

## Langerhans cell histiocytosis

* Description: : a rare disorder caused by clonal <u>proliferation</u> of <u>Langerhans cells</u> (<u>antigen</u>-presenting cells) [[11]](/library/uSYpYK)

* <u>Epidemiology</u>: : peak <u>incidence</u> between 5 and 10 years

* Clinical features

* Osseous lesions (90%): <u>pain</u> and/or swelling, <u>pathological fractures</u>

* Localization: <u>skull</u> (most common site), <u>femur</u>, <u>vertebra</u>, <u>mandible</u>, <u>ilium</u>, <u>ribs</u>
* Can cause recurrent <u>otitis media</u> if the mastoid bone is involved

* Unifocal or multifocal

* Systemic manifestations (less common)

* <u>Skin</u> <u>rash</u>: brown to purple <u>papules</u> and/or <u>eczematous</u> <u>rash</u>

* <u>Hepatomegaly</u> and/or <u>splenomegaly</u>

* <u>Lymphadenopathy</u>

* <u>Bone marrow</u> infiltration

* <u>Hypopituitarism</u> that typically manifests as <u>central diabetes insipidus</u>

* Exanthema

* Diagnostics

* Normal <u>calcium</u> levels

* <u>X-ray</u>: <u>osteolytic lesions</u> with or without marginal <u>sclerosis</u>

* <u>Biopsy</u> (<u>confirmatory test</u>): <u>proliferation</u> of <u>Langerhans cells</u> (polygonal cells with coffee bean-shaped <u>nuclei</u> and eosinophilic <u>cytoplasm</u>)  ;  [[12]](/library/ESY8YK)[[13]](/library/vSYAYK)

* <u>Electron microscopy</u>: Birbeck granules (tennis racket-shaped or rod-like structures) in the <u>cytoplasm</u>

* <u>Immunohistochemistry</u>: cells are positive for <u>S100</u>, <u>CD1a</u>, and/or CD207

* Treatment

* Solitary bone lesions in low-risk anatomical regions

* Asymptomatic lesion: A wait-and-watch approach may be appropriate.

* Symptomatic lesion: <u>curettage</u> and/or excision (as a part of <u>biopsy</u>)

* Bone lesions in high-risk anatomical regions (e.g., lesions involving the <u>odontoid process</u> or regions of the <u>skull</u> other than the vault), multifocal bone involvement, or systemic manifestation: <u>vinblastine</u> and <u>prednisone</u>
